> **What this case shows** — much of the ICF **d4 mobility** domain is everyday
> movement: walking, stairs, sitting, standing, lying. On the standard **UCI HAR**
> benchmark — 30 people, one waist smartphone — the ecosystem's dependency-free
> activity-recognition pipeline reaches **0.83** six-class accuracy on the
> provided subject-disjoint test split, and maps what it recognises to ICF codes
> (posture **d415**, walking **d450**, moving-around **d455**) — the real-world
> **performance** profile a clinic test cannot see. **What reproduces, and what
> doesn't** — the recognition reproduces on held-out subjects; the confusions are
> the physiologically expected ones — walking-**upstairs** vs downstairs (0.60),
> sitting vs standing (both static, separated only by orientation). Laying is
> perfectly separable (**1.00**). A simple 36-feature + k-NN pipeline is a
> **floor** (the literature reaches ~0.96 with 561 features + SVM), not a
> ceiling. **How to read it** — left, per-activity recall (blue = locomotion,
> green = posture, dashed = 0.17 chance); right, the ICF performance profile.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — the wearable-ADL pipeline at its most standard: **window** → HAR
**features** → **classify** → **map to ICF** — on the reference benchmark so you
can calibrate what "good" looks like.
**Way of thinking** — evaluate on the *provided subject-disjoint split* (never
mix a subject's windows across train and test), read accuracy against chance and
against the literature ceiling, and expect the confusions physiology predicts
(ascent/descent, sit/stand). A simple model sets the floor; report it as such.
**Ecosystem usage** — `adlFeatures()` → `trainADL()` / `recognizeADL()` →
`adlToICF()` (PhysioWearable); the classifier is swappable for PhysioML ROCKET
without touching the recipe.
:::

## Proposition

On the UCI HAR benchmark's provided subject-disjoint split, the HAR pipeline
reaches **0.83** six-class accuracy and maps the recognised locomotion/posture
activities to their ICF codes (d415 posture, d450 walking, d455 moving around).
Laying is perfectly recognised (**1.00**); walking-upstairs is the hardest
(**0.60**).

## Question & goal

**The question comes from the benchmark's design.** UCI HAR (Anguita et al. 2013)
was built as *the* public reference for recognising activities of daily living
from a smartphone: 30 people wore a waist phone through walking, ascending and
descending stairs, sitting, standing and lying, with a subject-disjoint train/test
split published so methods are comparable. We ask the benchmark's question and add
the clinical one: do the recognised activities map to the ICF mobility codes that
make them a *performance* measure?

## Challenge & approach

The challenge is set by the benchmark: generalise to **new people**, and separate
activities that share a signal — ascent from descent, sitting from standing. We
take each provided 128-sample window, extract the standard 36-feature descriptor,
train a dependency-free k-nearest-neighbours classifier on the training subjects,
and evaluate on the disjoint test subjects. `adlToICF()` maps the predictions to
ICF d-codes.

## Data

The **UCI HAR** smartphone accelerometer dataset (Anguita et al. 2013, UCI #240)
— 30 subjects, 50 Hz, six activities, provided train/test split. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Per-activity recall on the provided subject-disjoint test split (left; blue =
locomotion, green = posture, dashed = 0.17 chance) and the ICF performance
profile (right).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* every activity clears the chance line; laying is perfect,
upstairs is the weakest (confused with downstairs). On the right the recognised
time becomes an ICF mobility profile — posture-heavy, as expected for a mostly
sedentary benchmark day.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| 6-class accuracy (subject-disjoint) | **0.83** |
| walking (d450) recall / laying (d415) recall | 0.89 / 1.00 |
| walking-upstairs recall (hardest) | 0.60 |
| test windows (30-subject benchmark) | 2947 |

## Conclusion

A single waist accelerometer recognises the mobility and posture ADLs well enough
to build a real-world ICF performance profile — and does so on new people, with
the expected confusions and a clear headroom above a simple model. The
transferable takeaway: **benchmark on the provided subject-disjoint split, treat
a simple pipeline's number as the floor, and let ICF turn recognised activity into
a clinical performance picture.**

## Open questions

- Walking-upstairs is the weakest class (0.60), confused with downstairs; whether
  a richer feature set or barometer fusion resolves ascent vs descent is open.
  *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

The recipe is the standard wearable-ADL pipeline:

| step | function | package |
|---|---|---|
| window + extract HAR features | `adlFeatures()` | PhysioWearable |
| train / apply an activity recogniser | `trainADL()` / `recognizeADL()` | PhysioWearable |
| map activities to ICF performance codes | `adlToICF()` | PhysioWearable |

**Choosing the parameters:** use the sensor's native window (2.56 s at 50 Hz here);
always evaluate subject-disjoint; when you need the literature's accuracy, swap the
k-NN for `PhysioML::rocket()` + a classifier — the ICF mapping is unchanged. See
`adl-selfcare-hmp` / `adl-washing-htad` for the wrist-sensor siblings and
`adl-rasch-verbagg` for the capacity side.

```r
library(PhysioWearable)
feats <- adlFeatures(accel, sampling_rate = 50)
model <- trainADL(train_feats, train_labels)
adlToICF(recognizeADL(model, accel, sampling_rate = 50))   # ICF performance profile
```

[`artifacts/summary.csv`](artifacts/summary.csv),
